section_summary.extract_value: This section reports results for a male subsample (n=100), including factor-analytic procedures and reliability. Although initial eigenvalues suggested two factors, parallel analysis indicated only a single factor should be retained (first factor eigenvalue 4.18 vs. random 2.99), which explained 41.8% of the common variance, and scale reliability (Cronbach's alpha) was .84 (95% CI = .78–.88). The section also notes comparisons to the female subsample (e.g., loadings were more variable and only half the items reached "fair" loadings in men).
section_summary.evidence_source: Descriptive statistics for all 10 items for men (n=100) are reported Table 1.; The results of parallel analysis in the present study suggested that only a single factor should be extracted: only the first factor from the actual data had \lambda greater than the criterion \lambda generated from the random data (i.e., 4.18 [actual data] compared to 2.99 [random data] for the first factor, and 1.46 [actual data] compared to 2.17 [random data] for the second factor).; As such, we retained only the first factor, which explained 41.8% of the common variance.; Cronbach's alpha was .84 (95% CI = .78–.88), demonstrating internal consistency.

section_summary.extract_value: This section (3.1.2 Male subsample) reports results for the male subsample (n = 100). Factor analysis results for men showed adequate factorability (KMO = .88; Bartlett's χ2(45)=368.06, p < .001), parallel analysis supported a single factor (first λ = 4.18 > random 2.99; second λ = 1.46 < random 2.17) explaining 41.8% of common variance, item loadings were more variable than in the female subsample, and internal consistency was Cronbach's α = .84 (95% CI = .78–.88).

Asset Caption.extract_value:
Fig. 1. Path diagram and estimates for the one-dimensional model of the Body Appreciation Scale-2. The large oval is the latent construct, with the rectangles representing measured variables, and the small circles with numbers representing the unstandardized residual variables (variances). Error covariances were .14 for Items #2 and #9, .21 for Items #1 and #5, and −.16 for Items #4 and #7. The path factor loadings are unstandardised with significance levels determined by critical ratios (all p < .001).
